rules.title: FLSA — Hours Worked Standard

params.notes: Hours worked = time the employee is suffered or permitted to work; the Portal-to-Portal Act excludes ordinary commuting and activities preliminary or postliminary to the principal activity (incl. security screening, Integrity Staffing v. Busk 2014); 29 CFR 785.47 lets insubstantial, irregular minutes be disregarded

result.summary: Under the FLSA all time an employee is suffered or permitted to work is paid, except ordinary commuting and preliminary or postliminary activities excluded by the Portal-to-Portal Act; a de minimis exception exists.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Commute)

result.summary: Ordinary home-to-work travel is not hours worked, even to different worksites, unless the employee works during the trip.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Between Worksites)

result.summary: Travel between job sites during the workday, or from the employer's premises to the first site after reporting, is hours worked.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Special One Day Assignment)

params.notes: Employer may deduct the normal home-to-work commute time

result.summary: A special one-day assignment in another city is hours worked, less the time of the employee's normal commute.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Out Of Town)

result.summary: Overnight travel away from home is hours worked only during the employee's normal working hours (including corresponding hours on non-working days); passenger time outside those hours is unpaid unless work is done.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Employer Mandated Transport)

result.summary: Riding employer-provided transport from a meeting point to the worksite is not hours worked under the Portal-to-Portal Act unless the travel is itself a principal activity; several states (CA, NY, WA, MD, PA, MA) count it.

rules.title: FLSA — Restricted On-Call Time

params.test: engaged to wait: employee must remain on the premises or so close that the time cannot be used effectively for personal purposes

result.summary: An employee required to stay on or near the premises while on call is working and must be paid.

rules.title: FLSA — Unrestricted On-Call Time

params.test: waiting to be engaged: employee may leave a contact number and use the time for personal purposes
params.notes: Time actually spent responding to calls is paid

result.summary: An on-call employee who need only leave a contact number and can use the time freely is not working; only time responding to calls is paid.

rules.title: FLSA — Mandatory Training and Meetings

params.notes: Attendance is not voluntary if required or if the employee is led to believe non-attendance would hurt their job

result.summary: Required training, orientation and meetings are hours worked.

rules.title: FLSA — Voluntary Training Outside Hours

params.exclusion_test: all four: outside regular hours, genuinely voluntary, not directly related to the employee's current job, and no productive work performed
params.notes: Training to acquire a new or additional skill is not 'directly related'; apprenticeship instruction and independent courses are excluded

result.summary: Training is unpaid only when it is outside regular hours, voluntary, not directly related to the current job and involves no productive work; otherwise it is hours worked.

rules.title: FLSA — Time Clock Rounding

params.notes: Rounding to the nearest 5, 6 or 15 minutes is accepted where it averages out and does not fail to pay for all time actually worked over a period

result.summary: Punches may be rounded to the nearest quarter hour (or smaller increment) if the practice is neutral and does not, over time, fail to pay employees for all hours worked.

rules.title: California — Hours Worked Standard

params.notes: Control test (Morillion); no de minimis for regularly recurring minutes (Troester); mandatory on-site security checks are paid (Frlekin v. Apple 2020)

result.summary: California pays for all time the employee is subject to the employer's control, whether or not working; the Portal-to-Portal exclusions and the federal de minimis rule do not apply.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)

rules.title: California — Travel Time (Employer Mandated Transport)

params.notes: Optional employer-provided transport the employee may decline is not

result.summary: Time riding employer-required transport (e.g. a mandatory bus from a meeting point) is hours worked because the employee is under the employer's control.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)

rules.title: California — Travel Time (Commute)

params.notes: Commute in an employer vehicle with restrictions on personal use may be compensable

result.summary: An ordinary commute the employee controls is not hours worked; it becomes paid if the employer requires a particular route, vehicle or reporting point.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)
DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

rules.title: California — Travel Time (Out Of Town)

result.summary: All time spent travelling on employer-required out-of-town trips is hours worked, including as a passenger outside normal hours, less the normal commute; a lower agreed travel rate (at least minimum wage) may be set in advance.

citations.source: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

rules.title: California — Travel Time (Between Worksites)

result.summary: Travel between worksites during the day is hours worked.

citations.source: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

rules.title: California — Restricted On-Call Time

params.test: control test: degree of restriction on the employee's activities (Mendiola)
params.notes: Sleep time may be excluded only where a wage order expressly allows it

result.summary: On-call time on the employer's premises or under its control is hours worked, including sleep time on 24-hour shifts, because the employee cannot use it for their own purposes.

citations.source: Mendiola v. CPS Security Solutions, Inc., 60 Cal.4th 833 (2015)

rules.title: California — Mandatory Training and Meetings

result.summary: Required training, orientation and meetings are hours worked and the employer must bear their cost; a training rate lower than the regular rate (at least minimum wage) may be set in advance.

rules.title: California — Time Clock Rounding

params.notes: See's Candy (2012) allowed neutral rounding; Camp v. Home Depot review pending at the Supreme Court

result.summary: Neutral rounding survives only where the system does not capture exact time; meal-period punches may never be rounded (Donohue) and an employer that records exact punches must pay to the minute (Camp, Woodworth), so pay-to-the-minute is the safe practice.

citations.source: Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal.5th 58 (2021)
Camp v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 84 Cal.App.5th 638 (2022), review granted

params.exemptions: Establishments in partially exempt low-hazard industries (Appendix A to Subpart B) need not keep the log; all employers must report fatalities within 8 hours and in-patient hospitalizations, amputations or eye losses within 24 hours.
params.electronic_submission: Establishments with 20-249 employees in designated industries and 250+ employees submit 300A electronically; 100+ in designated industries also submit 300/301 data (since 2024).

result.summary: Employers with 11+ employees (outside partially exempt industries) must keep OSHA 300 logs and post the 300A summary; every employer must report severe injuries.

rules.title: California: workplace safety enforcement authority

params.agency: Cal/OSHA (Division of Occupational Safety and Health)
params.notes: State Plans may adopt stricter standards (heat, workplace violence, ergonomics, safety programs); see the state's other safety rules.

result.summary: California runs an OSHA-approved State Plan: private employers are inspected by Cal/OSHA (Division of Occupational Safety and Health) under state standards at least as effective as federal OSHA's.

citations.source: OSHA, State Plans: Frequently Asked Questions

rules.title: California: outdoor heat illness prevention

params.rest: shade at 80°F; 10-minute preventive cool-down rest every 2 hours at 95°F (agriculture)

result.summary: California outdoor employers must provide water, shade at 80°F, high-heat procedures at 95°F, acclimatization and a written heat illness prevention plan.

citations.source: Certainty Software, State Heat Illness Standards in 2026

rules.title: California: indoor heat illness prevention

params.rest: cool-down area kept below 82°F; preventive cool-down rest on request
params.notes: At 87°F (or 82°F with heavy clothing or radiant heat) employers must measure and record temperature and apply engineering or administrative controls.

result.summary: California indoor workplaces reaching 82°F must provide water, a cool-down area, training and a written plan; at 87°F controls and temperature records are required.

citations.source: Certainty Software, State Heat Illness Standards in 2026

rules.title: California: Injury and Illness Prevention Program (all employers)

params.notes: Written IIPP with responsibility, compliance, communication, hazard identification, investigation, correction, training and recordkeeping elements; employers with fewer than 10 employees may communicate orally and keep fewer records.

result.summary: Every California employer must maintain a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program.

citations.source: OSHA, Safety and Health Programs in the States (summary)

rules.title: California: workplace violence prevention plan (SB 553)

params.training: at plan implementation, annually, and when new hazards or changes arise
params.notes: Exempts healthcare covered by § 3342, employees teleworking from a location of their choice, and workplaces not open to the public with fewer than 10 employees present at a time. Violent incident log kept 5 years.

result.summary: Nearly every California employer must keep a written workplace violence prevention plan, train employees annually and maintain a violent incident log.

citations.source: Poster Compliance Center, Workplace Violence Laws: California and New York

rules.title: OSH Act § 11(c): retaliation for safety complaints prohibited

params.protected_activity: filing a safety or health complaint, participating in an inspection, refusing imminently dangerous work
params.notes: Complaints go to OSHA within 30 days; no private right of action.

result.summary: Employers may not discharge or discriminate against an employee for raising safety concerns or exercising OSH Act rights.

rules.title: FLSA § 15(a)(3): retaliation for wage complaints prohibited

params.protected_activity: filing a wage-hour complaint, oral or written, internal or to the Department of Labor; testifying in an FLSA proceeding
params.notes: Private right of action with back pay, liquidated damages and reinstatement.

result.summary: Employers may not retaliate against an employee for complaining about minimum wage or overtime violations.

rules.title: Title VII § 704(a): retaliation for opposing discrimination prohibited

params.protected_activity: opposing unlawful discrimination or participating in an EEOC charge, investigation or proceeding
params.notes: Parallel provisions in the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12203), ADEA (29 U.S.C. § 623(d)) and PWFA.

result.summary: Employers with 15+ employees may not retaliate against employees who oppose discrimination or take part in EEOC proceedings.

rules.title: NLRA § 7: protected concerted activity

params.protected_activity: employees acting together about wages, hours or working conditions, including discussing pay and raising group complaints, union or not
params.notes: Covers most private employers meeting NLRB jurisdictional thresholds; excludes supervisors, agricultural workers and independent contractors.

result.summary: Private employers may not discipline or restrain employees for concerted activity about working conditions, including discussing pay.

rules.title: California: whistleblower protection for private employees

params.notes: Protects internal or external disclosure of a reasonably believed violation of law, refusal to participate in a violation, and family members; § 1102.6 shifts the burden to the employer; § 1102.8 posting required.

result.summary: California has a general whistleblower statute covering private employers. Protects internal or external disclosure of a reasonably believed violation of law, refusal to participate in a violation, and family members; § 1102.6 shifts the burden to the employer; § 1102.8 posting required.

citations.source: Tate & Renner, State Whistleblower Law Chart

rules.title: California First Meal Break (>5 hours)

result.summary: 30-minute meal break for shifts of 5+ hours

rules.title: California — Meal Break Required (shifts > 5 hrs)

result.summary: California requires a 30-minute meal break for shifts over 5 hours. Ensure a break is scheduled.

rules.title: California Second Meal Break (>10 hours)

result.summary: 30-minute meal break for shifts of 10+ hours

rules.title: California — First Meal Period May Be Waived on Shifts of 6 Hours or Less

result.summary: When the total work period is no more than 6 hours the first meal period may be waived by mutual consent of employer and employee (Labor Code §512(a)). The consent need not be written but should be documented; the employee may withdraw it.

rules.title: California — First Meal Period Cannot Be Waived on Shifts Over 6 Hours (On-Duty Meal Only by Written Agreement)

result.summary: A first meal period on a shift longer than 6 hours cannot be waived. A paid on-duty meal period is permitted only when the nature of the work prevents relief from all duty and the parties have a written agreement that the employee may revoke at any time (Wage Orders §11). Otherwise a missed or late meal period owes one hour of premium pay (§226.7).

rules.title: California — Second Meal Period May Be Waived on Shifts of 10 to 12 Hours

result.summary: When the total work period is more than 10 but no more than 12 hours the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent, but only if the first meal period was not waived (Labor Code §512(a)). On shifts over 12 hours the second meal period cannot be waived outside the health care exception.

rules.title: Los Angeles — Offer Hours to Existing Employees Before Hiring

result.summary: Before hiring new employees or contractors, the employer must offer the work in writing to current employees for 72 hours (or until accepted) when they are qualified

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5 (offer of additional work) (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: Los Angeles — 14-Day Advance Notice Required (Retail)

result.summary: 1 hour of pay at the regular rate for each change the employer makes to a posted schedule with less than 14 days notice that adds time or changes the date, time or location with no loss of hours

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5, §185.00 et seq. (Fair Work Week Ordinance)
citations.section: LAMC Art. 5 (advance notice and predictability pay)

rules.title: Los Angeles — Schedule Change Premium (hours subtracted or shift cancelled with <14 days notice)

result.summary: Half the regular rate for each hour not worked when, with less than 14 days notice, the employer reduces a shift by at least 15 minutes or cancels it

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5 (predictability pay) (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: Los Angeles — Good Faith Estimate at Hire

result.summary: Before hire, and within 10 days of a request, the employer must give a written good faith estimate of the employee's work schedule

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5 (good faith estimate) (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: Los Angeles — On-Call Shift Premium (not called in)

result.summary: Half the regular rate for each scheduled hour of an on-call shift the employee is not called in to work

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5 (predictability pay) (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: Los Angeles — Right to Decline Late-Added Hours

result.summary: The employee may decline any hours, shifts or changes not on the posted schedule or added with less than 14 days notice; the employee's consent to a change must be in writing

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5 (right to decline) (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: Los Angeles — Fair Work Week: Right to Request Hours, Times and Locations; Written Reason for Denial

result.summary: A covered retail employee may request a preference for certain hours, times or locations of work. The employer may accept or decline, but a denial must state the reason in writing. Employee-requested changes do not trigger predictability pay.

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5, §185.03 (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: California Lactation Accommodation

result.summary: Reasonable break time to express milk, running with paid rest breaks where possible and otherwise unpaid; a private non-bathroom space is required (space-only hardship exemption under 50 employees)

citations.source: Cal. Labor Code §§1030-1034 (50-state survey used for encoding)

rules.title: California Rest Break (10 min per 4 hours worked)

result.summary: 10-minute rest break for shifts of 3.5+ hours

rules.title: California — Rest Break Required (per 4 hrs worked)

result.summary: California requires a paid 10-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked. Ensure rest breaks are scheduled.

rules.title: Federal Lactation Break Time (PUMP Act)

result.summary: Reasonable break time each time the employee needs to express milk for one year after the child's birth, in a private non-bathroom space; unpaid unless the employee is not fully relieved or uses a paid break (employers under 50 may claim undue hardship)

citations.source: Fair Labor Standards Act §18d (PUMP for Nursing Mothers Act)

rules.title: California Day of Rest (1 day off per 7-day workweek)

result.summary: Scheduling an employee to work more than 6 consecutive days without a day of rest. Employee may voluntarily choose to work the 7th day. Exemptions for emergencies and certain industries.

rules.title: Los Angeles — 10-Hour Rest Period (Retail)

result.summary: 1.5x pay rate for hours worked within the 10-hour rest period

citations.source: Los Angeles Municipal Code Art. 5, §185.00 et seq. (Fair Work Week Ordinance)

rules.title: California — Final Wages on Discharge

params.penalty: waiting time penalty of one day's wages per day late, up to 30 days (§203)

result.summary: All wages are due immediately on discharge or layoff; late payment accrues a waiting time penalty of a day's pay per day up to 30 days.

rules.title: California — Final Wages on Resignation

params.notice_shortens_deadline: due on the last day if the employee gave at least 72 hours' notice
params.penalty: waiting time penalty of one day's wages per day late, up to 30 days (§203)

result.summary: Employees who quit without 72 hours' notice are paid within 72 hours; with 72 hours' notice, on the last day.

rules.title: California: non-compete agreements

params.notes: Void regardless of where signed; employers had to notify affected employees in writing by 2024-02-14; employees may sue for injunctive relief and fees.

result.summary: California bans employee non-competes. Void regardless of where signed; employers had to notify affected employees in writing by 2024-02-14; employees may sue for injunctive relief and fees.

citations.source: Loio, Non-Compete Laws by State: 50-State Tracker (2026)
Non-Compete Checker, Non-Compete Laws by State (2026)

rules.title: Federal: FTC non-compete rule set aside

params.notes: The FTC's 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 910) was set aside nationwide in Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex., 2024-08-20) and the FTC dropped its appeal in September 2025; the agency pursues case-by-case enforcement under FTC Act § 5. State law governs enforceability.

result.summary: No federal rule bans non-competes: the FTC's 2024 rule was vacated, so state law controls.

citations.source: Ryan LLC v. FTC, No. 3:24-cv-00986 (N.D. Tex. Aug. 20, 2024)
Loio, Non-Compete Laws by State: 50-State Tracker (2026)

rules.title: California: separation and unemployment notice

params.document: Pamphlet DE 2320 'For Your Benefit' and written notice of change in employment relationship (plus HIPP notice)
params.deadline: by the effective date of separation (change notice immediately)
params.recipients: all discharged, laid off or leave-of-absence employees
params.notes: Section of the authority unverified; confirm the current form on the state agency site.

result.summary: California employers must give all discharged, laid off or leave-of-absence employees 'Pamphlet DE 2320 'For Your Benefit' and written notice of change in employment relationship (plus HIPP notice)' by the effective date of separation (change notice immediately).

citations.source: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 1089; Cal. Lab. Code § 2808(b); 22 CCR § 1089-1

rules.title: Federal: COBRA continuation coverage (20+ employees)

params.employer_scope: group health plans of employers with 20+ employees on more than 50% of business days in the prior year
params.notes: 18 months after termination or hours reduction (29 with disability, 36 for death, divorce or Medicare entitlement); plan administrator sends the election notice within 44 days; qualified beneficiaries get 60 days to elect and may be charged 102% of premium.

result.summary: Employers with 20+ employees must offer COBRA continuation of group health coverage for 18 to 36 months after a qualifying event.

rules.title: California: state health continuation (mini-COBRA)

params.employer_scope: employers with 2-19 employees (Cal-COBRA); also extends federal COBRA to 36 months
params.notes: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.20 et seq.; 60 days to elect. Applies to fully insured plans issued in the state; self-funded plans are governed by ERISA/COBRA only.

result.summary: California requires continuation of group health coverage for up to 36 months for employers with 2-19 employees (Cal-COBRA); also extends federal COBRA to 36 months. Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.20 et seq.; 60 days to elect.

citations.source: KFF, Expanded COBRA Continuation Coverage for Small Firm Employees
FindCoverage, Mini-COBRA State Law by State (2026)

rules.title: Federal: FLSA payroll records

params.records: payroll records, collective bargaining agreements, sales and purchase records

result.summary: FLSA payroll records: keep payroll records, collective bargaining agreements, sales and purchase records for 3 years.

rules.title: Federal: FLSA time cards and wage computation records

params.records: time cards, work schedules, wage rate tables, records of additions to or deductions from wages

params.records: applications, hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, layoff, termination, pay rate and training selection records; until final disposition of any charge

result.summary: Title VII / ADA / GINA personnel records (15+ employees): keep applications, hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, layoff, termination, pay rate and training selection records; until final disposition of any charge for 1 year.

rules.title: Federal: ADEA payroll and personnel records (20+ employees)

params.records: payroll records with name, address, birth date, occupation, pay rate and weekly compensation: 3 years; applications, job orders, test papers, physical exam results, promotion and layoff records: 1 year

result.summary: ADEA payroll and personnel records (20+ employees): keep payroll records with name, address, birth date, occupation, pay rate and weekly compensation: 3 years; applications, job orders, test papers, physical exam results, promotion and layoff records: 1 year for 3 years.

rules.title: Federal: FMLA leave records (50+ employees)

params.records: basic payroll data, dates and hours of FMLA leave, notices, policies, premium payments and disputes; medical records kept confidential and separate

result.summary: FMLA leave records (50+ employees): keep basic payroll data, dates and hours of FMLA leave, notices, policies, premium payments and disputes; medical records kept confidential and separate for 3 years.

rules.title: Federal: Form I-9 employment eligibility records

params.records: Form I-9 for each employee: 3 years after hire or 1 year after termination, whichever is later

result.summary: Form I-9 employment eligibility records: keep Form I-9 for each employee: 3 years after hire or 1 year after termination, whichever is later for 3 years.

rules.title: Federal: OSHA injury and illness records (11+ employees)

params.records: OSHA 300 log, 300A summary, 301 incident reports: 5 years after the year they cover

result.summary: OSHA injury and illness records (11+ employees): keep OSHA 300 log, 300A summary, 301 incident reports: 5 years after the year they cover for 5 years.

rules.title: Federal: OSHA employee exposure and medical records

params.records: exposure records 30 years; medical records for duration of employment plus 30 years

result.summary: OSHA employee exposure and medical records: keep exposure records 30 years; medical records for duration of employment plus 30 years for 30 years.

rules.title: Federal: Employment tax records

params.records: wages, tips, withholding, Forms W-4 and W-2, returns and deposits: 4 years after the tax is due or paid, whichever is later

result.summary: Employment tax records: keep wages, tips, withholding, Forms W-4 and W-2, returns and deposits: 4 years after the tax is due or paid, whichever is later for 4 years.

rules.title: Federal: Employee Polygraph Protection Act records

params.records: polygraph test records, reasons and notices where a test was administered under an exemption

result.summary: Employee Polygraph Protection Act records: keep polygraph test records, reasons and notices where a test was administered under an exemption for 3 years.

rules.title: California: payroll record retention

params.notes: Payroll records 3 years (4 years recommended for the UCL limitations period); employees may inspect or copy pay records within 21 days of request under § 226(c).

result.summary: California requires payroll and time records to be kept 3 years. Payroll records 3 years (4 years recommended for the UCL limitations period); employees may inspect or copy pay records within 21 days of request under § 226(c).

rules.title: California: employee access to personnel file

params.notes: Copies at the employee's cost; $750 penalty for non-compliance; pay records separately under § 226(c) within 21 days.

result.summary: California gives current and former employees a right to inspect their personnel file (reasonable intervals); response due 30 days after written request; copies must be provided. Copies at the employee's cost; $750 penalty for non-compliance; pay records separately under § 226(c) within 21 days.
